p: The same Hebrew letters can be read "I commanded" or "I was commanded." Ancient translations took the second.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex), with its vowel points
readings.en: as I commanded
readings.plain: just as I commanded

readings.w: Septuagint; also the Syriac Peshitta and Targum Pseudo-Jonathan, as reported by Milgrom (not checked in the original editions)
readings.en: as I was commanded
readings.plain: just as I was commanded

why: The consonants are identical; only the vowels, added by the Masoretes centuries later, differ. "I was commanded" matches Moses' words in 8:35 and 10:13, which may be why the ancient translators read it that way, but for the same reason it may be a smoothing. The Masoretic reading, with Moses speaking with God's authority, is kept, and the difference is small.

a: for yourself and for the people
t: For the people, or for his household?
p: The Greek has Aaron atone "for yourself and for your household," matching 16:6.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Samaritan Pentateuch
readings.en: for yourself and for the people
readings.plain: for yourself and for the people

readings.w: Septuagint (Greek, third century BC)
readings.orig: περὶ σεαυτοῦ καὶ τοῦ οἴκου σου
readings.en: for yourself and for your house
readings.plain: for yourself and for your household

why: The Hebrew mentions "the people" twice in the verse, and the Greek translator (or the Hebrew text he used) seems to have changed the first to "your household" to match 16:6, 11 and 17, and because Aaron's own offering (9:8–14) is for himself. That makes the Greek an easier, harmonized reading. The Masoretic text is followed. Hebrews 5:3 and 7:27, "first for his own sins, then for those of the people," fit either.
b: The Samaritan Pentateuch is listed with the Masoretic Text on the basis of standard reference works; I could not check it directly.

t: Moses commanded, or the LORD commanded Moses?
p: The Samaritan and Greek texts have the usual formula, "as the LORD commanded Moses."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
readings.en: as Moses commanded
readings.plain: just as Moses commanded

readings.w: Samaritan Pentateuch and Septuagint, as reported in BHS and by Milgrom (not checked directly)
readings.en: as the LORD commanded Moses
readings.plain: just as the LORD commanded Moses

why: Everywhere else in chapters 8–9 the formula is "as the LORD commanded Moses" (8:9, 13, 17; 9:10), so the longer reading looks like a scribe filling in the familiar phrase. The shorter Masoretic reading is the harder one and fits 9:5–6, where Moses passes on the command. It is followed.

p: The written Hebrew has "his hand"; the scribes' reading tradition says "his hands."

readings.w: Qere (the reading the Masoretes marked to be read aloud); Septuagint; nearly all translations
readings.en: his hands
readings.plain: Aaron lifted his hands

readings.w: Ketiv (the consonants written in the Leningrad Codex)
readings.en: his hand
readings.plain: Aaron lifted his hand

why: The written form may be an old spelling of the plural, as also happens at 16:21. The Masoretes' reading "his hands" agrees with the old translations and with later practice, in which priests raise both hands to bless (Mishnah Sotah 7:6).

a: those that have jointed legs above their feet
p: The written text says lo' ("not"); the scribes read lo ("to it"), "which have legs."

readings.w: Qere (the Masoretes' reading); Septuagint; all translations
readings.en: which have jointed legs
readings.plain: those that have jointed legs above their feet

readings.w: Ketiv (the consonants written in the Leningrad Codex)
readings.en: which do not have jointed legs
readings.plain: those that do not have jointed legs above their feet

why: The two words sound the same in Hebrew (lo), and are confused several times in the Bible (compare 25:30; Isaiah 9:3). "Not" makes no sense here, since the point is that locusts have leaping legs. The Qere is certainly right; the Ketiv is a spelling slip or an old spelling.

p: The Greek, a Qumran scroll and the Samaritan text have a longer verse. The Hebrew may have skipped a line.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
readings.orig: רָר בְּשָׂרוֹ אֶת־זוֹבוֹ אוֹ־הֶחְתִּים בְּשָׂרוֹ מִזּוֹבוֹ טֻמְאָתוֹ הִוא
readings.en: whether his flesh runs ... or is stopped ..., it is his uncleanness
readings.plain: it is his uncleanness.

readings.w: Septuagint; 11QpaleoLev-a (Dead Sea scroll in the old Hebrew script, dated by Freedman and Mathews to about 100 BC, a date others dispute); the Samaritan Pentateuch is reported to agree (not checked directly)
readings.orig: טמאתו היא בו כל ימי זב בשרו או החתים בשרו מזובו טמאתו היא
readings.en: ... it is his uncleanness in him; all the days his flesh runs or his flesh is stopped from his discharge, it is his uncleanness
readings.plain: it is his uncleanness. He is unclean all the days his flesh runs or his flesh is stopped up from his discharge. It is his uncleanness.

why: The longer text repeats "his flesh is stopped up from his discharge, it is his uncleanness." A copyist's eye could easily have jumped from the first to the second occurrence and left out the words between (called homoioteleuton, "same ending"). Emanuel Tov and others think that is what happened in the Masoretic line, so the longer text may be original. The Plain English Translation follows the Masoretic Text, as the KJV, ESV and NIV do, since the meaning is the same either way. I have not checked every modern version; some committee translations that weigh the scrolls may adopt the longer text.

a: when they drew near before the LORD and died
p: The Greek adds what their approach was: "when they brought strange fire before the Lord."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Samaritan Pentateuch
readings.en: when they drew near before the LORD and died
readings.plain: when they drew near before the LORD and died

readings.w: Septuagint; similar wording in the Targums
readings.orig: ἐν τῷ προσάγειν αὐτοὺς πῦρ ἀλλότριον ἔναντι κυρίου καὶ ἐτελεύτων
readings.en: when they brought strange fire before the Lord and died
readings.plain: when they brought strange fire near before the LORD and died

why: The Greek fills in the reason from 10:1 and Numbers 3:4. That is an explanatory addition, the kind of help translators often gave. The shorter Hebrew is followed; its vaguer "drew near" fits the warning that follows about coming near at the wrong time.

p: The written Hebrew has "his hand" with the word "two"; the Masoretes read "his hands."

readings.w: Qere (the Masoretes' reading); Septuagint; all translations
readings.en: his two hands
readings.plain: both his hands

readings.w: Ketiv (the consonants written in the Leningrad Codex)
readings.en: his two hand (an old spelling of the plural?)
readings.plain: both his hand

why: With the number "two" the meaning is certain. The written form is probably an older spelling of the plural, as at 9:22. The detail matters because two hands here contrast with the one hand leaned on ordinary offerings (1:4), which David P. Wright read as a difference between transfer and ownership.

a: he is to present a flawless male.
t: The leaning of the hand repeated
p: The Greek adds "and he shall lay his hand on its head," repeating 1:4 for the sheep or goat.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
readings.en: he shall present a flawless male
readings.plain: he is to present a flawless male.

readings.w: Septuagint (checked in a printed Greek text online; not checked in Wevers' Göttingen apparatus)
readings.orig: ἄρσεν ἄμωμον προσάξει αὐτὸ καὶ ἐπιθήσει τὴν χεῖρα ἐπὶ τὴν κεφαλὴν αὐτοῦ
readings.en: he shall bring a flawless male and lay his hand on its head
readings.plain: he is to present a flawless male and lean his hand on its head.

why: The Greek fills in the gesture so that the flock offering matches the herd offering (1:4). A translator or scribe adding the familiar step is far more likely than a Hebrew scribe dropping it, so the shorter text is followed. Either way the rabbis assumed the hand was leaned on every animal offering of an individual.

p: The Greek, and reportedly the Samaritan text, call the community's bull "flawless," as in 4:3.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
readings.en: a bull of the herd
readings.plain: a young bull

readings.w: Septuagint (checked in a printed Greek text online); the Samaritan Pentateuch is reported to agree (not checked directly)
readings.en: a flawless calf of the herd
readings.plain: a flawless young bull

why: Every offering had to be flawless, so the meaning does not change. The longer reading matches 4:3 and looks like harmonizing; the shorter Hebrew is followed.

a: there is no black hair in it
t: No black hair, or no yellow hair?
p: The Greek reads "no yellowish hair," as in 13:30 and 13:32. Many commentators think the Hebrew is the harder reading.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
readings.en: and there is no black hair in it
readings.plain: there is no black hair in it

readings.w: Septuagint (checked in a printed Greek text online)
readings.orig: θρὶξ ξανθίζουσα οὐκ ἔστιν ἐν αὐτῇ
readings.en: there is no yellowish hair in it
readings.plain: there is no yellow hair in it

why: The two verses around it speak of yellow hair, so the Greek is smooth, and some scholars emend the Hebrew to match. But the Hebrew can make sense: black hair is the sign of healthy skin (13:37), so a patch that is not deep but also has no healthy hair is doubtful and must be shut away. The harder Masoretic reading is followed.

a: And he did just as the LORD commanded Moses.
p: The Greek has no report that Aaron did it. It reads "once a year it will be done, as the Lord commanded Moses."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
readings.en: and he did as the LORD commanded Moses
readings.plain: And he did just as the LORD commanded Moses.

readings.w: Septuagint (checked in a printed Greek text online)
readings.orig: ἅπαξ τοῦ ἐνιαυτοῦ ποιηθήσεται, καθὰ συνέταξε Κύριος τῷ Μωυσῇ
readings.en: once a year it will be done, as the Lord commanded Moses
readings.plain: It will be done just as the LORD commanded Moses.

why: The Hebrew suddenly reports that someone, probably Aaron, carried out the rite, though the chapter sets it for the seventh month (16:29) and the book's calendar puts the inauguration in the first month (Exodus 40:17). The Greek avoids that problem by making it part of the command. That smoother reading looks secondary; the harder Hebrew is followed, and the note on 16:34 discusses it.
